Falling house prices due to a 'number of factors', Treasurer says
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is being asked about the government's housing tax changes in relation to falling house prices.
ICYMI, house prices fell for a sixth straight month in September, bringing cumulative declines to 5.2 per cent below March's peak.
Experts say house prices could drop about 15 per cent in the coming months amid rising inflation and interest rate hikes.
Chalmers has been asked if the government's reforms are working as intended.

He said house prices were on a similar level to November last year — suggesting the prices had flattened — and added that there were multiple factors that contributed to lower prices, including interest rates and broader economic conditions.

The changes in the budget are designed to make it more afforable for first home buyers, he said, adding that extraordinary price growth over the past 20 decades had locked young people out of the market.
"Housing is the defining intergenerational challenge," he said. "Prices started to come off before the budget, and that's because there are a number of factors at play."
"Housing is the defining intergenerational challenge," he said.
"Prices started to come off before the budget, and that's because there are a number of factors at play."
Treasurer asked about Minns's comments on government spending
Treasurer Jim Chlamers has been asked about comments from NSW Premier Chris Minns yesterday about government spending.

Minns, a Labor premier, yesterday said his own government had been "careful with public money", and he declined to defend Chalmers when asked about the accusation that federal spending was contributing to rising inflation and interest rates.
Chalmers appeared to suggest Minns was speaking in general terms about all governments.

"The premier of NSW made the same sorts of points that we have been making, which is that there is an onus on all governments at all levels to manage their budgets in the most responsible way that they can," Chalmers said.
"As I understand it, he was referring to demand in the economy."
He said public demand growth had "slowed considerably".

"And so Chris, as I understand it, was talking about demand, talking about the role that every government has to make sure they're managing the budget in the most responsible way they can, and that's what we're doing. "
Treasurer hails ban on 'annoying' surcharges
Jim Chalmers is spruiking the end of "pesky" credit and debit card surcharges incurred when consumers tap to pay.
He said the move would ease pressure on people in a tough economic environment, adding that surcharges cost $1.6 billion a year.
"What you see on the menu is what you pay when you tap your card," he said.
"This is about easing the cost of living … this is about the end of those annoying, pesky surcharges that everyone has paid in one way or another."
Chalmers said the Reserve Bank of Australia would implement the change, while the small business ombudsman would help small businesses adapt.
"We'll make sure that everybody's doing the right thing. The ACCC's got an important role to play in that regard," he said.
But he said if small businesses raise prices in response, they'll need to justify it and put it on the menu.
Treasurer announces $134m investment in crisis housing

The government will invest $134 million in crisis transition housing for families experiencing domestic and family violence, and for young people at risk of homelessness, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said today.

Speaking at a press conference earlier while the PM was speaking, Chalmers said there had been some difficult reminders recently about the "horrific impact" of domestic and family violence in the community.
He said that issue was tightly linked to housing and homelessness.
He says the scheme will give people a "safe and secure place to rebuild their lives".
He said the funding would build more than 200 homes across Queensland, and was expected to help 20,000 families and 5,000 young people at risk of homelessness over the next 20 years.
PM sidesteps question on union plan to levy AI companies
Unions and researchers are pushing for tech giants that want to build data centres in Australia to be slugged with a levy to help fund a local artificial intelligence (AI) industry.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has sidestepped the question and says the government is engaging constructively with AI companies, including internationally based ones.
"AI does have risks, but it also has potentially enormous benefits for humankind to lift the quality of life, to boost productivity of businesses, including ones here," the PM says.
And that's the end of the PM's press conference from Tasmania.
Albanese says rising fuel prices have wider inflationary impact
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says rising fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East have a flow-on effect on other goods and services.
Headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in August, from 3.5 per cent in July, driven by higher housing costs and automotive fuel prices.
The Reserve Bank of Australia on Tuesday raised interest rates for the fourth time this year to 4.6 per cent.
"It has an inflationary impact … right around the world, which is why we continue to call for a de-escalation," Albanese says.
Albanese says it's 'concerning' new Greens leader has attacked Labor
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has congratulated new Greens leader David Shoebridge for his election to the party's leadership.
Following his election, Shoebridge says he wants the Greens to replace Labor and doesn't want to help the government improve.
The PM says it was "somewhat concerning" that Shoebridge used the opportunity to criticised Labor amid the rise in One Nation.

"Sounded a lot like some of the people who didn't win their seats at the House of Representatives election last May," the PM said, referring to the three Greens MPs who lost their seats at the last election.
PM doesn't think Minns's comments on spending equate to a swipe
The prime minister has been asked about comments from NSW Premier Chris Minns yesterday on the Commonwealth's handling of the budget.
Yesterday, Minns said he had "long" heard advice from the Reserve Bank to rein in spending and, when asked, declined to support the federal government's fiscal approach.
But questioned whether he thinks the premier has taken a swipe at the Commonwealth, Albanese says: "No".
Albanese says negative gearing changes will lead to more house supply
The PM has been asked whether the government's budget changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax are working as he wanted.

Australian house prices fell for a sixth straight month in September, and experts say the property market could experience falls of up to 15 per cent in the coming months off the back of higher interest rates and cuts to housing tax breaks.
Anthony Albanese says the budget changes will allow more people to get into the housing market.
He says the changes to limit negative gearing to new builds will help with housing supply in Australia.

"That will help to build supply. Now that doesn't happen within a month or two months or three months of the new financial year. That will happen over a period of time, and that will lead to an increase in supply," Albanese says.

Asked what he would say to people who have taken up Labor's five per cent deposit scheme and have fallen into negative equity, Albanese says fewer people are in negative equity compared to the former Coalition government.
PM says govt expects smelter to deliver strong returns initially
The prime minister has moved to questions now, where he's asked about the package and what it entails.
Anthony Albanese says the $200 million is split evenly between the Commonwealth and Tasmanian governments.
He says the government expects the high price of aluminium will deliver the smelter strong returns initially.

"We've been absolutely determined to drive a deal that is in the interests of taxpayers, the Commonwealth, the state, but also in the interest of the company that has to obviously make a return on its investment," Albanese says.
Industry Minister Tim Ayres says the deal, which takes the plant to 2030, includes providing the aluminium smelter with hydro power.
He says the $200 million to Rio Tinto, which manages the plant, includes a cap on expenditure each year and thresholds to protect investment.
Albanese announces $200 million bailout of Bell Bay aluminium smelter
Anthony Albanese has just stepped up to speak at the Bell Bay smelter to announce the joint Commonwealth-Tasmanian government bailout.
The $200 million bailout of the aluminium smelter will support 550 direct jobs and 1,000 indirect jobs in the area.
Accompanied by the Tasmanian premier, the prime minister says both governments have worked in the interest of Australians and Tasmanians.
"I want to say this to Jeremy Rockliff as well, publicly, what I say to him privately: We work together. There's no party lines here," Albanese says.
"I thank you, Jeremy, for the spirit in which you engage consistently, not just in this area but in education, in health, in other areas as well."
Albanese says he wants Australia to become more self-reliant and improve resilience, which he says is "vital" for the nation.
Rockliff says the bailout is vital for the Tasmanian economy and effectively amounts to a $5 billion injection into the area.
Labor warns education providers against trying to 'game' student visas
There has been a rush of enrolments into a graduate diploma days before it was due to shut down amid concerns that international students were using it to remain in Australia.

More than 1,300 students joined the Graduate Diploma of Management (Learning), and the commencement date of a further 1,500 students was brought forward to circumvent a looming deadline for its cancellation.

The federal government has written formal letters of concern to a number of VET providers asking them to explain the surge in new students in the weeks since it was announced the course would be shuttered on October 5.
Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill said the message to providers, agents and students was: "Do not try to game this measure."
"A paper enrolment, a rushed orientation or token activity is not a licence to evade the intent of the action and curious patterns are now being actively examined," he said.
Hill said students should be "very wary" of anyone pressuring them to start another course immediately, particularly while they were still completing their studies.
"Genuine students deserve clear advice and quality education — not arrangements created for someone else's commercial benefit," he said.
Shoebridge commits to timeframe for direct election of Greens leader
New Greens leader David Shoebridge has committed to ensuring the party's leadership is directly elected by members.
NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi, who contested the party leadership yesterday and lost, said she was frustrated members didn't get a vote.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast earlier, Shoebridge says the party will work through what that model looks like.
He says he's committed to having the model in place and a vote occur after the next federal election, which is scheduled for early 2028.

"We'll work through what that model looks like and we are committed to having that in place for the next vote and the next vote will be under our rules immediately following the next federal election," Shoebridge says. "It's a pretty clear timeframe, a commitment from Steph [Hodgins-May] and myself to make sure members get in a direct say."

"We'll work through what that model looks like and we are committed to having that in place for the next vote and the next vote will be under our rules immediately following the next federal election," Shoebridge says.
"It's a pretty clear timeframe, a commitment from Steph [Hodgins-May] and myself to make sure members get in a direct say."
Ayres says Shoebridge looks to continue 'aggressive, hyperpartisan' politics
Tim Ayres says it appears the new Greens leader wants to continue an "aggressive, hyperpartisan" style of politics.
NSW senator David Shoebridge was elected as Greens leader yesterday, defeating fellow NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi.
Following his election, Shoebridge says he wanted the Greens to replace Labor and didn't want to make the government better.
The industry minister told ABC News Breakfast that Labor won't be focused on the Greens.

"Well, we'll work carefully across the parliament and the Senate to secure support for legislation that matters in the national interests," Ayres says. "We won't engage in kind of slanging matches on television with Senator Shoebridge."
"Well, we'll work carefully across the parliament and the Senate to secure support for legislation that matters in the national interests," Ayres says.
"We won't engage in kind of slanging matches on television with Senator Shoebridge."
Bailout of Bell Bay smelter an 'important intervention', Ayres says
Tim Ayres says the joint federal and Tasmanian government bailout of the Bell Bay smelter buttresses Australia's industrial capacity.
The Commonwealth and Tasmanian governments have announced a $200 million bailout of the aluminium smelter that will be split 50:50.
The industry minister has told ABC News Breakfast it's an "important intervention" that's expected to support 550 direct jobs and 1,000 indirect jobs in the area.

"Each of these deals are calibrated carefully to make sure that we are protecting the fiscal interests of the government, but most of all they are about making Australia stronger and more resilient," Ayres says.

"It's about securing our current industrial capacity and making sure that we extend the kind of industrial capabilities that Australia needs and our regional economies and our outer suburbs need to make our economy strong."

Burns dismisses swipe from NSW premier
Federal Labor MP Josh Burns has dismissed comments from the NSW premier about the Commonwealth's management of the budget.
Yesterday, NSW Premier Chris Minns said he had "long" heard advice from the Reserve Bank to rein in spending and, when asked, declined to support the federal government's fiscal approach.
It comes after the Reserve Bank hiked interest rates for the fourth time this year on Tuesday, and inflation rose to 4 per cent.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Burns says the NSW premier is looking at how to best manage his state's economy.

"Our job is to manage the economy across the country. I do think that we obviously want to align fiscal and monetary policy. That's obviously really important and inflation is a really difficult problem," Burns says.
Key Event
New Greens leader plays down concerns expressed by leadership contender
David Shoebridge says he doesn't think it's true NSW Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi doesn't want to work with him following yesterday's leadership vote.
Faruqi, who lost the leadership vote 7–4, said she didn't run for deputy leadership because she believed she could play her part "outside the constraints of the leadership team".
She said she was frustrated the leadership was not elected by Greens members.
But Shoebridge has spoken to ABC Radio National Breakfast, playing down her concerns, and says Faruqi is free to campaign on the issues that matter to her.

"I am looking forward to Senator Faruqi, Mehreen, getting out there campaigning on matters that she's clearly got a passion for and a talent to connect with big parts of this country," Shoebridge says.
Shoebridge says ballot for party leader shows 'strength' of Greens
Greens leader David Shoebridge says he thinks his party's decision to break with tradition and have a leadership ballot yesterday is a sign of the strength of the Greens.
The party held its first leadership ballot yesterday, with the vote coming down 7–4 to Shoebridge and NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi in the second round of voting.
The Greens have previously chosen its leader by consensus.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Shoebridge says he thinks yesterday's vote shows the party's strength.
"At a moment like this, if there wasn't a contest, if we didn't have a bunch of people desperate to take on and meet this moment, I think it wouldn't be true to politics in 2026," Shoebridge says.
$200 million funding package announced for Bell Bay Aluminium smelter
The Australian and Tasmanian governments have announced a $200 million support package for the Bell Bay Aluminium smelter after months of uncertainty.

The smelter's future had been looking shaky with its owner, multi-billion-dollar company Rio Tinto, locked in protracted negotiations with the state-owned power company Hydro Tasmania over a new power deal.
There were fears the smelter, which employs 550 people, would shut if a new deal was not reached before it expired at the end of the year.
The state government has now announced Rio and Hydro have struck a five-year power deal.

Watt accuses new Greens leader of coming from 'angry, militant' faction
Murray Watt has urged new Greens leader David Shoebridge to take a more constructive approach to dealing with Labor in parliament.
Shoebridge defeated fellow NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi and SA senator Sarah Hanson-Young for the party's top job yesterday.
Yesterday, Shoebridge told the media that he wanted his political party to replace Labor.
The environment minister told Channel Seven that Shoebridge comes from the Greens' "angry, militant faction" and urged him to be constructive.

"We certainly hope that Senator Shoebridge can take a more constructive approach to working with the parliament and working with the government than he's shown to date," Watt says. "I really hope for the Greens sake that it's not a return to the bad old days, where they just wanted to block everything."
"We certainly hope that Senator Shoebridge can take a more constructive approach to working with the parliament and working with the government than he's shown to date," Watt says.
"I really hope for the Greens sake that it's not a return to the bad old days, where they just wanted to block everything."
